description: From Cartier-Bresson to Nick Ut, the press photo captures history in one image. Freedom, ethics and power of the media in the same viewfinder.

hero.hook: A photo can stop a war… or lie. We still need to be able to publish it.

blocks.text: Photographic journalism is born when the image fixes the news as strongly as an article. A single view can sum up a war, a famine, a victory.
But without press freedom, these images remain in a drawer.

theorizes the “decisive moment”: being in the right place, at the right time, with the right framing. , alongside Capa, died covering the Spanish Civil War. Photojournalism has its martyrs. [[Henri Cartier-Bresson]] [[Gerda Taro]]
The appearance of illustrated magazines and photo agencies professionalized the profession. The reporter leaves with a device like others with a notebook. The risk is physical.

blocks.caption: The Leica on the shoulder: the street as terrain.

blocks.text: In Vietnam, 's photo showing a little girl burned by napalm shakes public opinion. The image does not “end” the war alone, but it makes the human cost impossible to deny. [[Nick Ut]]
Large democracies theoretically protect the press. Dictatorships control the viewfinder. The freedom to publish an image becomes a political barometer.
Many famous photos were first censored or discussed before becoming historical evidence.
asks questions: can we frame suffering? Retouch? The  also threatens the free gaze. [[The ethics of photojournalism]] [[Media concentration and editorial independence]]
In the digital age, verification is essential: metadata, reverse image search, context. Photography remains powerful, but it can be manipulated faster than ever.

blocks.caption: The reporter: witness armed with an objective.

blocks.text: In the age of networks, everyone takes photos. The need for reliable, contextualized images, protected by the right to information, has never been so strong.
To fully understand press freedom and photographic journalism, you must keep one thing in mind: each technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never just decorative.
Context matters as much as style. Dates, places, sponsors, public: all this explains why a form appears at a specific moment, and not before.
Finally, legacy is measured over the long term. What we see today in museums, films or popular music still bears the traces of these inventions.
Train the eye, defend whistleblowers, pay for field journalism: without this, all that remains is the flow. The heritage of the 20th century is a requirement, not a nostalgia.
From Cartier-Bresson's Leica to war photos, photojournalism has proven that a free image can carry as much weight as an editorial.
